q.intro.text: A drone flies in a straight line from A to B on a map. Each grid unit is one mile. How far does it fly? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one. The picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s0.text: Go across from A, then up to B. The corner C is a right angle, because grid lines are perpendicular. So A B is the hypotenuse.

e.s1.text: The legs are how far you move. The run is nine minus three, six. The rise is twelve minus four, eight.

e.s2.text: A B squared is six squared plus eight squared: thirty six plus sixty four, one hundred.

e.s3.text: A B is the square root of one hundred: ten miles. It is longer than each leg, and shorter than the trip around the corner. A sensible size.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why are the legs six and eight, and not nine and twelve?

e.why-ok.text: Yes. A leg is how far you move from A to B: nine minus three across, and twelve minus four up.

e.why-coord.text: Nine and twelve say where B is, measured from the origin, not from A. That triangle would start at zero, zero.

e.why-add.text: Adding the coordinates gives no distance at all. Distance along a line is a difference, so subtract.

t.intro.text: Now in three D. A box is three inches by four inches by twelve inches. How long is the longest stick that fits, from corner A to corner G? The first triangle is done for you.

t.tri.text: A G goes through the inside of the box. Which right triangle has A G as its hypotenuse?

t.tri-ok.text: Yes. A C on the floor, C G straight up, A G across. The right angle is at C, because C G is perpendicular to the whole floor.

t.tri-floor.text: A B C lies flat on the floor. Its hypotenuse is the floor diagonal, A C. A G also climbs the height.

t.tri-front.text: A B F lies on the front face. Its hypotenuse is A F, a face diagonal, not A G.

t.sq.text: In triangle A C G, the legs are A C, five, and C G, twelve. What is A G squared?

t.sq-ok.text: Yes. Twenty five plus one hundred forty four is one hundred sixty nine.

t.sq-face.text: Twenty five is the floor diagonal squared. A G also climbs twelve inches, so add twelve squared.

t.sq-add.text: That adds lengths. Square the legs first: five squared plus twelve squared.

t.sq-no.text: Square each leg, then add. Five times five, plus twelve times twelve.

t.len.text: A G squared is one hundred sixty nine. How long is A G?

t.len-ok.text: Yes. The square root of one hundred sixty nine is thirteen inches. A thirteen inch stick just fits, corner to corner.

t.len-root.text: One hundred sixty nine is A G squared. The length is its square root. Which number times itself makes one hundred sixty nine?

t.len-half.text: A square root is not half. Eighty four and a half times itself is far more than one hundred sixty nine.

t.len-face.text: Five is the floor diagonal, A C. A G climbs twelve inches more, so it is longer.

t.len-add.text: Adding lengths walks along the edges. The straight stick is shorter.

t.len-no.text: Which number times itself makes one hundred sixty nine?

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked ten miles, and you were right. On the plane and in a box it is the same move: find the right triangle, square, add, take the root.

t.cb-add.text: At the start you picked fourteen miles. That is the trip along the grid. The straight line is shorter: the squares add, not the lengths.

t.cb-coord.text: At the start you picked fifteen miles. That used the coordinates of B as the legs. The legs are how far you move: six and eight.

t.cb-none.text: Find the right triangle, square, add, take the root. On a map, in a box, anywhere.

p.intro.text: Lena’s triangle has sides five, twelve and thirteen, and twenty five plus one hundred forty four is one hundred sixty nine. Lena says: a right triangle gives a squared plus b squared equals c squared, so the equation gives a right triangle. Rules work backward. Is her reason good?

p.flip.text: Test it. A square has four right angles. Backward it fails: a two by five rectangle has four too. So the converse needs a proof. Pick each reason.

p.build.text: Right. Rules do not always flip. So prove the converse: pick each reason.

p.c1.text: Right. Draw a right angle, and mark five and twelve along its sides.

p.c2.text: Right. The new triangle is right, so its hypotenuse is the square root of one hundred sixty nine: thirteen.

p.c3.text: Right. Same three sides: it fits exactly on Lena’s triangle.

p.no-flip.text: That is the reason we just tested. Rules do not always flip.

p.no-looks.text: Looks are not a reason. Eighty nine degrees looks square too. Use the three lengths.

p.no-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That proves the converse. Same legs, the theorem gives the hypotenuse, and same three sides give the same right angle.
